demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
Arun describes his life before the accident with a kind of wistful precision, the way one might describe a meticulously organized spreadsheet that has since been corrupted. He was a man who found comfort in rules, in the clear debit and credit of a tax return. For twenty years, his world was governed by logic and predictable outcomes. He would leave for work at 7:15 a.m., review audits with unwavering focus, and return home to his wife, Priya, at 6:00 p.m. It was a life of quiet order, and he was content in its rhythm.

That order was irrevocably shattered on a Tuesday afternoon eighteen months ago. The sun was low and bright, a blinding glare off the windshield of the car in front of him. He was thinking about a complex capital gains case, inching through a residential intersection. He remembers the light turning green, the slight pressure of his foot on the accelerator. He never saw the boy on the scooter. The first thing he registered was the sound—not a crash, but a heavy, organic thud that seemed to vibrate through the steering wheel into his bones. Then, a flash of red from the boy’s jacket, and the sight of the scooter skittering across the pavement.

In the seconds that followed, Arun’s world of numbers and rules dissolved into pure, primal terror. He remembers stumbling out of his car, the smell of hot asphalt, and the sight of the boy’s leg bent at an angle that was fundamentally wrong. He remembers the mother’s scream, a sound he says has permanently rewired his brain. The boy survived, but the damage was severe and lasting. The police report cleared Arun of any legal fault; it was a tragic, unavoidable accident. But that verdict offered no solace. In his own mind, he was convicted of a crime for which there is no penance.

Now, at forty-two, Arun is a ghost in his own life. He no longer drives. The car keys sit in a bowl by the door, untouched. His commute is now a ninety-minute ordeal of trains and buses, a journey he feels he deserves. Any sudden, sharp sound—a dropped book, a car backfiring on the street below his office—sends a jolt of ice through his veins, his heart hammering against his ribs as if trying to escape. He sees the boy’s face constantly. It appears in the reflection of his computer monitor, the image of wide, terrified eyes just before the impact. It’s there when he closes his eyes to sleep, ensuring that rest is a rare and fleeting visitor.

His work, once a source of pride, has become a place of torment. The intricate details of the tax code, the very things he used to master, now feel impossible to grasp. He will read the same sentence a dozen times, the words blurring into meaningless shapes. He makes small, careless errors he never would have made before, and each one feels like another piece of evidence confirming his incompetence, his worthlessness. He feels a profound and suffocating shame, a sense that he is a monster masquerading as a man in a suit.

He and Priya barely speak anymore. He sees the worry in her eyes but cannot meet her gaze. How can he accept her comfort when he feels he deserves none? He feels disconnected from her, from his home, from the man he used to be. He describes it as watching his life through a thick pane of glass. He is present, but he cannot feel anything beyond the cold, heavy weight of guilt that settled in his chest the moment he heard that thud. It is the first thing he feels when he wakes up and the last thing he knows before a night of broken sleep.
